regcompR: Distributional Regression in R

regcompR fits distributional regression models: every parameter of a response distribution (location, scale, shape, zero inflation, cure fraction, ordinal thresholds, copula dependence) can depend on covariates through its own formula, and random effects can enter any of them. One model specification runs on several engines:

  • maximum or penalized likelihood, with a Laplace approximation for random effects and smooth terms;
  • automatic differentiation and the Laplace approximation of TMB, through RTMB;
  • Bayesian inference with generated Stan programs (run by bayescompR, cmdstanr or rstan) or BUGS programs (run by JAGS or OpenBUGS).

Distributions live in a machine readable registry of 278 families. Each entry records its support, parameter domains and links, moments with the conditions under which they exist, the methods available on each engine, references, and its validation status. Operators build new families from registered ones, and every family, built or registered, works in every part of the package.

Installation 

# Development version
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("adamrsophie/regcompR")

regcompR needs R 4.3.0 or later. It contains no compiled code of its own. Optional engines need their own packages: RTMB for engine = "tmb", a Stan runner (cmdstanr, rstan or bayescompR), or JAGS with R2jags for engine = "bayes".

Quick start 

library(regcompR)
set.seed(2026)

# Distribution objects
length(families())
#> [1] 278
d <- distribution("nb2", mu = 4, phi = 2)
prob(d, 0:3)
#> [1] 0.1111111 0.1481481 0.1481481 0.1316872
quantile(d, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
#> [1] 0 3 9
c(mean = mean(d), variance = variance(d))
#>     mean variance
#>        4       12

# A negative binomial model with a random intercept in the mean and a
# regression on the dispersion, fitted through TMB
n <- 500
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(n), g = factor(rep(1:50, each = 10)))
dat$y <- rnbinom(n, mu = exp(1 + dat$x + rnorm(50, 0, 0.4)[dat$g]),
                 size = exp(0.3 + 1.2 * dat$x))
fit <- regcomp(y ~ x + (1 | g), phi ~ x, family = "nb2", data = dat,
               engine = "tmb")
round(coef(fit), 3)
#>  mu:(Intercept)            mu:x phi:(Intercept)           phi:x
#>           0.940           1.104           0.393           0.890
round(exp(fit$theta), 3)       # random intercept standard deviation
#> mu:1 | g:log_sd((Intercept))
#>                        0.261

# Predictive quantiles and event probabilities for a new group
nd <- data.frame(x = c(0.2, 0.8))
predict(fit, nd, type = "quantile", probs = c(0.1, 0.9), re = "zero")
#>      q0.1 q0.9
#> [1,]    0    7
#> [2,]    1   12
predict(fit, nd, type = "probability", at = 0, re = "zero")
#>      probability(0)
#> [1,]     0.16123603
#> [2,]     0.03444051

# Operators give new families, used like any other
zinb <- regcomp(y ~ x, zi ~ 1, family = inflate("nb2"), data = dat)
AIC(fit, zinb)
#>      df      AIC
#> fit   5 2557.586
#> zinb  4 2571.487

# Diagnostics
plot(fit, which = c("rootogram", "qq", "ranef"))

# The same model in Stan
fit_b <- regcomp(y ~ x + (1 | g), phi ~ x, family = "nb2", data = dat,
                 engine = "bayes")

What is covered

Area Highlights
Registry 278 families: count, binary, finite discrete, bounded, ordinal, nominal, real line, positive, unit interval, simplex, circular and directional, extreme value, multivariate and matrix valued; density, distribution function, quantile, random generation, moments, score and Hessian for each
Count data Poisson, NB1, NB2, NB-P, generalized Poisson, Conway Maxwell Poisson, Poisson inverse Gaussian, Poisson lognormal, Sichel, Delaporte, generalized Waring, generalized negative binomial, Faddy’s extended Poisson process models, multivariate counts; zero truncated, zero inflated and hurdle variants
Operators inflate(), hurdle(), truncate_dist(), censor(), transform_dist(), discretize(), round_dist(), mixture(), compound(), convolve_dist(), splice(), cure(), copula_dist(), wrap(), weighted(), skew symmetric constructions, and generators such as Kumaraswamy G, beta G, Marshall Olkin, transmuted and exponentiated families
Regression A formula for every parameter, offsets, weights, custom links, fixed parameters, smooth terms through mgcv bases, penalties (ridge, lasso, elastic net, adaptive lasso, group lasso, SCAD, MCP) and bias reduction (Firth, FLIC, FLAC, log F)
Hierarchical models Random intercepts and slopes in any parameter, nested and crossed factors, correlated or independent effects, multiple membership terms
Longitudinal models AR(1), compound symmetry, unstructured, diagonal, Ornstein Uhlenbeck and spatial (exponential, Gaussian, Matern 3/2) covariance structures; GEE with independence, exchangeable, AR(1) and unstructured working correlations; cluster robust covariances
Ordinal and categorical Cumulative (logit, probit, cloglog, loglog, cauchit), continuation ratio, adjacent category and stereotype models, location scale ordinal models, multinomial logit, bivariate binary odds ratio and sample selection models
Survival Right, left and interval censoring, truncation and delayed entry for any family; parametric survival models; mixture cure models; discrete time hazards with person_period() and frailty through random effects
Special methods Exact conditional Poisson regression, quantile regression for counts, custom families from a log density
Inference and prediction Wald and posterior summaries, sandwich covariances, predictions of the mean, any parameter, quantiles, probabilities and survival with confidence or credible intervals, conditional or marginal over random effects
Checking and comparison Randomized quantile residuals, PIT histograms, rootograms, effect and caterpillar plots, posterior predictive checks, log, CRPS, Dawid Sebastiani, Brier and ranked probability scores, K fold cross validation, identifiability checks
Bayesian backends Generated Stan code for every family with a Stan density, all random effect structures and multiple membership; BUGS code for JAGS and OpenBUGS; priors by class, parameter and coefficient

family_capabilities() reports what each engine supports for a family, and registry_table() returns the whole registry as a data frame.

Validation

  • Families are checked for normalization, for agreement between its density, distribution function and quantile function, and for moments against simulation; families with a reference implementation are compared with it (stats, extraDistr, VGAM, actuar, evd, circular and others).
  • Model fits are tested against established packages on the same data: linear and generalized linear mixed models against lme4 and glmmTMB, covariance structures against glmmTMB, ordinal models against MASS, ordinal and VGAM, multinomial models against nnet, GEE against geepack, sandwich covariances against sandwich, parametric survival against survival, cure models against flexsurvcure, copulas against copula, and scoring rules against scoringRules.
  • The TMB engine reproduces the default engine’s estimates and standard errors; Bayesian fits are checked against the likelihood fits.
  • R CMD check --as-cran passes with no errors or warnings.

Citing regcompR 

citation("regcompR")

The repository ships machine readable citation metadata:

  • CITATION.cff: Citation File Format (GitHub “Cite this repository”, Zenodo).
  • .zenodo.json: Zenodo deposit metadata.
  • inst/CITATION: the R level citation (citation("regcompR")).

Once the first GitHub release is archived on Zenodo, its concept DOI will resolve to the latest release.

Contributing

Bug reports, feature requests, and pull requests are welcome; see CONTRIBUTING.md. A wrong answer is the most useful bug report: include a reproducible example and, if you can, what a reference package returns for the same model. Please follow the Code of Conduct, and report security issues privately as described in SECURITY.md.

Acknowledgments

regcompR builds on the distributional regression framework of Rigby and Stasinopoulos (2005), on TMB (Kristensen et al. 2016) through RTMB, and on Stan, JAGS and OpenBUGS for Bayesian inference. The packages used as references in its tests are gratefully acknowledged.
